title: Dev dashboard — seven decisions before I draw it
intro: You asked for a YouCoded dev dashboard: one page that launches dev servers from any branch and runs our check suites. Before I design it, seven questions. Everything below is about what YOU would see and do — none of it is about code. Facts I checked first, so the questions make sense: there are 24 separate copies of the app on this machine right now (the main one plus 23 branch copies, one per in-flight piece of work); your app is currently on the 'Golden Sunbreak' theme, and I can read that theme's exact colours, corner radius, wallpaper and blur settings from an ordinary file on disk without ever touching your running app.

sections.title: How it gets built and where it runs

questions.today: There is no dashboard. To launch a dev copy of the app you tell me a branch name and I type a command; to run the checks I type a different command. You see none of it except my summary afterwards.
questions.problem: You can't see what's runnable, what's already running, or what passed — and you can't start any of it yourself. Everything routes through me typing.
questions.proposal: Build the dashboard as a page you open in your browser at a fixed web address. The question is what it's made of, because that decides how much extra work it is later to move it inside YouCoded as a real Settings screen.

options.label: A small standalone page, hand-built to look like YouCoded
pros: Fastest to get in your hands — working today rather than after a build-out
Genuinely functional from minute one: buttons really launch things
Reads your live theme file, so it looks like your app without being your app
cons: When it later becomes a real Settings screen, the look carries over but the plumbing is rewritten
It is a dev tool on your machine, not something other users would ever see

options.label: Build it as a real YouCoded screen from the start, served on its own address
pros: Looks exactly like the app because it IS the app's screen, theme switching and all, for free
Moving it into Settings later is mostly deleting the standalone wrapper
cons: Slower to first use — the app's screen machinery has to be stood up before a single button works
Heavier to run: it boots a chunk of YouCoded just to show you a list of branches

options.label: Mock it up in the workbench first, build the working version after you approve the look
pros: You see and shape the layout before anything is wired up
Matches how we do new app features
cons: Nothing works during the mockup stage — the buttons are painted, not live
Two rounds before you can actually use it, and you said you want to use and test it

questions.today: Your app is on 'Golden Sunbreak'. When you switch themes, the app changes; nothing else on your machine does.
questions.problem: A dev page that ignores your theme looks like a foreign tool bolted on. You asked for it to match the active theme.
questions.proposal: The dashboard reads the same theme file your app reads and paints itself to match. The question is how far that goes.

options.label: Follow your active theme automatically, colours and shapes only
pros: Switch themes in the app, reload the dashboard, it has followed — no setting to keep in sync
Reads plainly and loads instantly; nothing heavy in the background
cons: No wallpaper or frosted-glass blur, so side by side with the app it will look flatter
If you're running two themes' worth of work at once it always shows the one your app is set to

options.label: Follow your active theme fully — colours, shapes, wallpaper, blur
pros: Sitting next to your app it looks like it belongs to it
Still automatic — no picker to remember
cons: Wallpaper and blur behind a dense table of branches can make text harder to scan
Slightly heavier page; on a big list you may notice it when scrolling

options.label: A theme picker on the dashboard itself, defaulting to your active theme
pros: You can put the dashboard in a plain high-contrast theme while the app stays pretty
Doubles as a quick way to eyeball how a theme's colours read on a dense screen
cons: One more control on a page you asked to be as minimal as possible
It can drift out of step with the app and look wrong for no obvious reason

sections.title: Launching dev copies of the app

questions.today: I run a command naming a branch; a separate 'YouCoded Dev' window opens on your desktop. If two of them collide on the same port one of them gets killed silently. Nothing tracks which ones are open.
questions.problem: You can't see what's running, you can't stop one without asking me, and after a long day there can be several open with no way to tell which branch each one is.
questions.proposal: The dashboard lists every branch copy and gives each a Launch button. The question is how much it manages after launch.

options.label: Launch only — the dashboard opens windows, you close them yourself
pros: Simplest thing on screen: a list of branches and one button each
Nothing to go wrong; closing a window works the way it always has
cons: No way to tell from the page which branches are already open
Launching the same branch twice can silently kill the first window

options.label: Launch and track — each row shows Running or not, with a Stop button
pros: One glance tells you what's open and on which branch
Stop from the page instead of hunting for the right window
Ports and profiles get picked for you, so two instances can't collide
cons: The page has to keep checking in the background, so it is never fully idle
If a window is closed the normal way, the row takes a moment to notice

options.label: Launch, track, and label the windows so they match the page
pros: Every open window's title says which branch it is, matching the row you clicked
Easiest to keep straight when four are open at once
cons: Nothing extra to go wrong, but it is more moving parts than the simplest version
Window titles are set at launch, so one you started before today's dashboard won't be labelled

questions.today: When I launch a dev copy, a real window appears on your desktop, sometimes while you're doing something else. I warn you in chat first.
questions.problem: A dashboard button that silently paints a window over your work would be worse than the current warning.
questions.proposal: Decide what a Launch click does before the window appears.

options.label: Click launches immediately — you clicked it, you expect a window
pros: Fastest; one click, no ceremony
You are already looking at the dashboard, so nothing is a surprise
cons: A stray click opens a whole app window and takes focus off what you were doing
Takes 10-20 seconds to appear, so a mis-click is slow to undo

options.label: Click starts it and the row says 'starting…' — the window is not brought to the front
pros: You keep your place; the window appears behind and waits for you
The row tells you it worked, so you don't click twice
cons: A window you asked for opening behind your work can feel like nothing happened
You have to go find it in the taskbar

questions.today: We have several separate check suites. The fast one takes about ten seconds and catches most mistakes. There's a whole-app screenshot sweep that takes five minutes. There's an Android one. There's a docs-accuracy audit. There's a paid one that asks real AI models to use the app's tools and grades them, at roughly 25 cents per run.
questions.problem: None of them are discoverable — you'd have to remember they exist and ask me by name.
questions.proposal: Put buttons on the dashboard for a set of them, per branch. The question is how big that set is to start.

options.label: The fast safety check only, per branch
pros: One button, one answer: is this branch safe or not
Ten seconds, so you'll actually use it
Nothing on the page you'd never press
cons: Says nothing about Android, about how the app looks, or about whether the docs still match
You'd still ask me for the others by name

options.label: The free ones: fast safety check, Android tests, docs audit, and the workbench boot check
pros: Everything that costs nothing but time is one click away
Covers the two blind spots the fast check openly admits to — Android and docs
cons: Four buttons per branch is more page than one button per branch
Android takes minutes, so a mis-click ties up the machine for a while

options.label: All of them, with the paid one clearly marked and asking to confirm the spend
pros: Nothing hidden — the full toolbox, including the screenshot sweep and the model evaluation
You could start a paid model evaluation yourself instead of asking me
cons: Real money is one confirm-click away on a page you might browse casually
The screenshot sweep runs several browsers at once for five minutes and will slow the machine down

questions.today: When I run a check, I see pages of output and hand you a one-line verdict. You never see the raw output unless something goes wrong.
questions.problem: If you press the button yourself, you need to know it's working and what it found — but the raw output is mostly noise.
questions.proposal: Decide what the page shows while a check runs and after it finishes.

options.label: A verdict line, with the full output behind a 'show details' toggle
pros: Normal case is one calm line: passed, or failed with the count
The detail is there when you want it and out of the way when you don't
Keeps the page as minimal as you asked
cons: While it's running you see a spinner, not progress, so a slow one feels stuck
For a failure you'll usually still want me to read the details and explain

options.label: Live scrolling output as it runs, collapsing to a verdict when it's done
pros: You can see it is genuinely working, not hung
For the slow suites, watching progress is reassuring
cons: Scrolling technical output is exactly the jargon you don't want on screen
Busier page; harder to have three branches checking at once without it feeling chaotic

sections.title: What else earns a place on the page

questions.today: There are 23 branch copies of the app on disk right now. Some are finished and merged weeks ago, some hold work that exists nowhere else. Nothing on your machine tells them apart, and one of them recently sat holding the only copy of four days of work while looking exactly like a finished one.
questions.problem: You have no view of what's in flight, what's safe to delete, and what would be lost forever if deleted. That is the most dangerous gap here.
questions.proposal: Beyond launching and checking, add one more thing to each branch row. Pick the one you'd get the most from — I'll build one now and we can add more later.

options.label: Status: is it saved, is it pushed, is it merged, would deleting it lose work
pros: Directly answers 'is this finished, and is it safe to clean up'
Flags the dangerous case — work that exists only on this disk — in red before you touch it
Turns a list of 23 cryptic names into something you can actually act on
cons: Reading 23 branches' status takes a couple of seconds when the page loads
It tells you what's safe to delete but doesn't delete it — that stays a conversation with me

options.label: What the branch is about — the last few changes in plain language, and any design doc for it
pros: Answers 'what even is leu-t13-manifest' without asking me
Makes the list browsable rather than a wall of codenames
cons: Change descriptions are written by me for me, so some will still read as jargon
Doesn't warn you about anything — it's context, not safety

options.label: A running-processes panel: every dev server and stray browser this machine has open, with ports and a Stop button
pros: Cleans up the leftovers that block the next launch
Answers 'why is my machine slow' in one glance
cons: It is about the machine, not about your work, so you'd look at it rarely
A Stop button next to a list of processes is the easiest way on this page to kill something you wanted
